title: Demonstrate an understanding of vine frame development

lessons.title: The parts of the vine frame
lessons.html:
The parts of the vine frame

The frame is the permanent woody shape of the vine. It is built in the first years after planting and is then kept for the life of the vine. A good frame makes the vine strong, gives an even crop and makes pruning and picking easy.

Parts of the frame

  • Trunk: the straight main stem from the ground to the cordon wire.
  • Head: the top of the trunk, where the arms start.
  • Cordons (arms): the woody arms that grow along the cordon wire, usually one to each side.
  • Spurs: short pieces of one-year-old wood with a few buds, left on the cordon at pruning. New shoots and bunches grow from them.
  • Canes: longer one-year-old shoots, used instead of spurs on some cultivars and systems.

Why the frame matters

Good framePoor frame
Straight trunk, cordons level on the wireBent trunk, cordons hanging or crossing
Spurs evenly spaced along the cordonGaps in some places, crowding in others
Even crop, good air flowUneven crop, more disease
Easy to prune and pickSlow, difficult work

Words to know

  • Bud: a small growing point on the shoot or cane. It grows into a new shoot.
  • Node: the place on a shoot where a leaf and bud grow.
  • Lateral: a side shoot that grows from a main shoot.
  • Sucker: a shoot growing from the trunk below the head or from the rootstock. Suckers are removed.

Your supervisor will show you the frame shape your farm uses. Each block may be different.

lessons.title: Building the frame year by year
lessons.html:
Building the frame year by year

Building a frame takes about two to three seasons. The exact steps depend on the farm, but the main idea is the same.

Year 1: growing the trunk

  1. After planting, let a few shoots grow. When they are long enough, choose the strongest, straightest one.
  2. Remove the other shoots.
  3. Tie the chosen shoot loosely to the stake every 20 to 30 cm as it grows, so it stays straight.
  4. Remove suckers and laterals low on the trunk as instructed.

Winter pruning after year 1

If the shoot is strong and has reached the cordon wire, it is cut a little below the wire, at the height your supervisor gives. If it is weak or short, it is cut back to two buds and grown again next season. A weak trunk is never forced up to the wire.

Year 2: forming the cordons

  1. Let shoots grow from the top buds just below the wire.
  2. Choose the best two shoots, one for each side. These become the cordons.
  3. Bend them gently onto the cordon wire and tie them loosely. Do not twist them tightly around the wire; the wire can cut into the wood as it thickens.
  4. Remove the other shoots on the trunk.

Year 2 to 3: setting the spurs

As the cordons grow along the wire, shoots grow upwards from them. At winter pruning, keep evenly spaced shoots and cut them back to short spurs with the number of buds your farm uses. Remove shoots in between. The aim is spurs spaced evenly along the whole cordon, on the top side.

Good practice

  • Use sharp, clean secateurs and make clean cuts.
  • Tie with soft ties that will not cut the wood.
  • Do not let young vines carry a heavy crop while the frame is being built.
  • Fix problems early. A badly placed arm is hard to correct later.

Key points

  • The frame is the permanent shape of the vine: trunk, head, cordons and spurs.
  • Year 1: grow one strong, straight shoot up the stake for the trunk.
  • A weak trunk is cut back and grown again, not forced to the wire.
  • Year 2: train two shoots along the wire as cordons, tied loosely.
  • Set evenly spaced spurs along the cordon and remove suckers.
